architecture.html.title: Architecture and rendering pipeline | Simple3D
architecture.html.summary: Architecture and rendering pipeline Simple3D provides software and native GPU rendering for opaque 3D scenes inside ordinary .NET MAUI pages. You describe geometry and a camera in Core. The MAUI control selects a native Metal/GLES surface or a software bitmap surface, overlays labels through SkiaSharp, and connects pointer gestures to the camera and selection. Package boundaries Component Responsibility Dependencies Simple3D.Core Shapes, immutable meshes, hierarchy, camera, projection, depth rasterization and picking .NET 10 / System.Numerics Simple3D.Maui SceneView, gestures, caching, bitmap presentation, selection and label layout Core, MAUI, SkiaSharp Your application Scene content, animation timing, selected-part details and layout MAUI control, or Core alone for exports Gallery Five examples using shared scene factories Both libraries through the demo project Core has no MAUI or SkiaSharp dependency. You can render and query pixels in a console app without a native UI. SceneView is a ContentView containing native GPU and Skia surfaces. The software path uses SKCanvasView for bitmap presentation; the hardware path executes triangles on Metal or GLES3. See hardware rendering. This boundary keeps geometry and rendering tests portable. Your page hosts a normal MAUI view without adopting a game engine's application lifecycle. One software frame, step by step Invalidate. Scene and camera mutations raise synchronous notifications. The view marks cached output dirty and requests a paint. An unchanged native paint can reuse its previous target. Flatten and validate. Core traverses groups iteratively, composes child and parent transforms, and collects geometry leaves. Repeated instances count separately. Node and triangle limits bound preparation. Transform and shade. Each triangle moves to world coordinates. Core rejects degenerate triangles, applies optional back-face culling, and computes diffuse color from configurable world-space directional and ambient light. Mesh normals enable per-vertex Gouraud shading; otherwise lighting remains flat. Unlit materials bypass lighting. Clip and project. Points move into camera space. Core clips triangles against the near plane, then projects with perspective or orthographic math. It bounds each projected triangle to the viewport. Rasterize. At each covered pixel center, Core compares interpolated depth with the nearest stored depth. A nearer triangle writes color and its leaf-shape ID together. Perspective uses reciprocal depth; orthographic mode uses linear depth. Equal-depth samples retain the earlier shape. Present. The view copies changed pixels into a reusable Skia bitmap, optionally filters diagonal edges, adds selection tint and contour, and scales to the native surface. It draws labels afterward, with bounds and overlap handling. Scratch depth storage belongs to the DepthRenderer instance. Color and shape-ID arrays belong to the frame or reusable target. Core projects labels separately; labels overlay geometry without depth testing. Software picking shares visibility A render records the winning leaf ID for each pixel. Pick looks up that ID and returns its shape without a second geometry pass. Hidden triangles cannot win a tap. SceneView.PickAt maps layout coordinates into target pixels. Selection uses the same ID buffer, preserving occlusion without changing materials. Shape replacement transfers selection to the corresponding child position in the new tree. Keep logical child order stable during animation; removed or missing parts clear selection. Ownership and repeated frames API Storage lifetime Typical use DepthRenderer.Render / SceneView.CaptureFrame Owned pixels and pick data survive later renders Export, screenshot, tests DepthRenderer.RenderInto Fixed-size RenderTarget reuses color and ID arrays; the next call overwrites content Animation and native painting Reuse a target at the same size and share immutable meshes between shape replacements. Core reads triangles by index, avoiding a separate triangle enumerator for each leaf. Each renderer reuses its flattened-node storage; capacity follows the largest prepared scene, while shape references are cleared after success or failure. Picking snapshots retain their own shape arrays. Traversal, shape arrays and labels still allocate; reuse does not mean zero allocation. A failed RenderInto invalidates picking and may leave partial pixels. Render successfully before reading that target again. A renderer instance is not thread safe because it shares depth and traversal scratch storage. Mutate and render a scene on the same thread; use the UI thread with SceneView. On native handler disconnect, the view releases subscriptions and rendering resources. Snapshots held by your application remain valid. Responsiveness and bounded work Core caps dimensions at 2,048 pixels, traversal at 100,000 node visits, aggregate triangles at 1,000,000, and raster bounding-box samples at 16,000,000 per frame. These are resource bounds, not recommended animation workloads. See Rendering limits. During pan or pinch, the view caps the longest render dimension at 512 pixels and restores configured detail after the gesture. If raster work exceeds the budget, native painting retries at half resolution and avoids probing an expensive full-size frame on every animation update. MaximumRenderDimension lets the application set an animation budget. Your application owns animation timing. Replace shapes from a UI timer and stop it when the page disappears. Cost grows with covered pixels and overlap as well as triangle count. Profile the native target and distinguish CPU render time from displayed frame rate. Deliberate scope The software path keeps rendering, visibility and picking in one inspectable pipeline. Its tradeoff is CPU work per covered pixel. Simple3D supports opaque textures, flat or smooth diffuse lighting, vertex colors, and OBJ geometry import. It has no transparency, PBR or shadows. Attribute interpolation is perspective-correct, including across near-plane clipping. SceneRenderer is the older projected-triangle API, retained for compatible primitive/default-camera code. SceneView uses DepthRenderer for software presentation and explicit snapshots. Use the depth path for custom meshes, newer camera features and intersecting geometry. examples.html.title: Five examples to learn from | Simple3D
examples.html.summary: Five examples to learn from Create the two-shape scene in Getting started first, then follow these five examples in order. Each adds a different API concept, progressing from primitives to a mechanism with coordinated moving parts. Each file creates a scene, fits its camera and supplies a time-based animation. The gallery adds orbit, zoom and selection through the same SceneView you use in an app. The texture, lighting, normals, vertex-color and OBJ examples require 0.2.0-preview.1 or later. Example and source What to learn Motion Equipment Named primitives and groups; an OBJ controller with UV-mapped display Output vector sweeps Telemetry Orthographic camera and data-driven height and color Bars change within a fixed scale Surface Height-based vertex colors, flat/smooth normals and directional light controls Sample marker follows a wave Robot Arm Nested transforms and selectable joints Shoulder and elbow articulate Gantry Crane Linked motion with fixed structure and reusable geometry Carriage traverses while the hoist lifts its load In Equipment, orbit the controller beside the motor: the chart belongs to a mapped front face, while the solid sides reveal the imported enclosure's depth. ObjReader.Parse imports the wedge and its independent UV indices once. A small opaque Texture2D supplies its display and body colors. The texture is generated in the shared sample so Core-only image exports need no codec; use TextureLoader.Load in a MAUI app to decode an image once before creating the material. In Surface, choose Shading (Smooth / Flat), then Light from (Left / Right). Smooth mode uses averaged vertex normals; flat mode omits normals from the same wave geometry. Both keep the height gradient and 512 triangles, so the comparison isolates lighting rather than changing mesh detail. The light-ray direction changes in world space while the orbit camera stays put. SurfaceComparison.cs keeps both meshes and lights prepared; switching does no geometry generation and preserves selection. Reset restores smooth shading, light from the right, the initial camera and sample-marker position. The comparison controls appear only in Surface, above its description. Telemetry and Gantry Crane use synthetic values, not live sensors or physical simulations. In an application, replace the time functions with measured values. Reuse immutable meshes and keep child order stable so selection follows the same logical part after replacement. The small shared helpers live in DemoScenes.cs. Robot Arm demonstrates child transforms relative to a parent. Gantry Crane combines group translation with state-dependent part dimensions: the cable changes length as the load rises. They teach different uses of the same hierarchy API. The examples share their animation and color helpers rather than repeating them in each file. The gallery page owns the UI timer, lowers render resolution during animation and pauses on backgrounding. It targets 60 updates per second; this is not a displayed-frame-rate guarantee. Press Animate after returning to the app. Mirror The gallery's Mirror card opens a full-screen scene in which a character copies the person the camera sees, in portrait or landscape. Everything runs on the device; nothing is recorded or sent. Start. The intro explains the three framings, then asks for the camera. Get in frame. A silhouette shows where to stand: whole body, waist up, or just the face for close-up face tracking. Play. The character appears and copies the person. Tap a thumbnail to switch characters, ⇄ to switch cameras, pinch to zoom. If the person leaves, a hint asks them back; haptics mark both moments. What it follows: Body: arms, legs, torso bend and lean, turning toward or away from the camera (the back shows when they turn around). Arms stay outside the torso and pass behind it when a hand is hidden. Face: mouth, each eye, smile and frown, through each character's own face table, so a wide-open mouth looks wide open on every model. Head: turn, nod and tilt. Smoothness: poses arrive at camera rate (25–30 Hz) and are eased at the display's rate (FrameClock, up to 240 Hz). The whole pipeline costs about 0.03 ms of CPU per displayed frame. Cat Juanita CosmicBot Froggy Each character's neutral face, open mouth, left and right blink, smile and frown (Froggy blinks with both eyes and has no smile or frown). Tested on real people The tests replay Apple Vision landmarks from public-domain videos of real people through the full pipeline and every character (sources): Video Checks NASA astronaut candidate Anna Menon talking (NASA/JSC) Mouth follows hers (r = 0.91) and opens 7–15% of head height on every character; blinks close the eyes; head turn follows (r = 0.89) Medical officer Sudha in an interview (NIOSH/CDC) Head tilt and turn follow (r = 0.81, 0.88) Half squats, filmed at an angle (CDC) Tracked in every frame; hips drop with hers; knees bend 60–114° at the bottom; the character turns to her angle Seated overhead press (CDC) Hands above the head whenever hers are, and below it whenever hers are lowered, in every frame The people shown do not endorse this project. Piece Source Tracking states, smoothing, face calibration PoseTracker.cs Landmarks → humanoid bone rotations HumanoidRetargeter.cs Face measurements FaceGeometry.cs Per-character face tables MirrorFace.cs, MirrorModels.cs Pose easing and expressions MirrorSession.cs Pond stage, character placement, swaps MirrorStage.cs Camera, detectors and page Simple3D.Demo/Mirror To reproduce it in your app, load a VRM with GltfLoader, wrap it with MirrorCharacter.FromVrm (optionally with a MirrorFace table), feed PoseFrames from your detector into MirrorSession.Apply, and call MirrorSession.Present from a FrameClock tick; the shared folder has no MAUI or platform dependencies. Detection runs on the device: Apple Vision is built into iOS and macOS; on Android, ML Kit's accurate pose and face models arrive with their NuGet packages. Detectors report 2D landmarks, so motion straight toward the camera is approximate. The characters are CC0 VRMs from ToxSam and Polygonal Mind's 100Avatars; see skinned characters. The GIF is rendered from the recorded landmarks with --render-showcase and paired with the source videos by scripts/mirror-showcase.py. Render without MAUI dotnet run --project tests/Simple3D.Core.Tests -c Release -- --render-images Equipment equipment.ppm dotnet run --project tests/Simple3D.Core.Tests -c Release -- --render-images --all output This exports initial still frames as binary PPM and skips the test run. Convert them to PNG with python3 scripts/render-doc-images.py to regenerate the documentation images. Rendering supports opaque textured triangles and flat or smooth directional lighting; see limits before choosing a workload.

getting-started.html.title: Getting started | Simple3D
getting-started.html.summary: Getting started Requirements Use .NET 10 with the target's MAUI workload and an iOS, Android or Mac Catalyst app. Windows is not supported; remove a Windows target from a default MAUI project before restoring. Apple builds require macOS and a workload-compatible Xcode. Install the MAUI package from NuGet.org: dotnet add YourApp.csproj package Simple3D.Maui --version 0.3.0 For a local-feed build, follow packaging. Core is a transitive dependency. For a source checkout, reference src/Simple3D.Maui instead. Core-only applications can install Simple3D.Core without MAUI workloads. Register the SkiaSharp handler in the host app: using SkiaSharp.Views.Maui.Controls.Hosting; var builder = MauiApp.CreateBuilder(); builder.UseMauiApp<App>().UseSkiaSharp(); In a ContentPage, create a scene and show it: using Simple3D.Core; using Simple3D.Maui; var scene = new Scene() .Add(Shape.Box(0xFF8DA9FF).Named("Case").At(-0.7f, 0, 0)) .Add(Shape.Sphere(0xFFFFB775).Named("Ball").At(0.7f, 0, 0)); var view = new SceneView { Scene = scene, HeightRequest = 320 }; view.Camera.FitToScene(scene, aspectRatio: 4f / 3); Content = view; For a display-only scene, set IsInteractive = false. This removes the view's orbit, pinch and tap gestures. The default is interactive; you can switch the property at runtime. The camera can still be changed in code. For simple animation, replace immutable shapes on the UI thread. Each replacement invalidates the frame. Set MaximumRenderDimension to a smaller physical size while animating to bound the software rasterizer's per-frame work, then restore it when the animation stops. The gallery demo gives each scene its own time-based motion. Its timer targets 60 updates per second and stops when the page disappears or its window enters the background (Window.Stopped). Returning to the app leaves it paused until Animate is pressed. Ignore already queued ticks after stopping a timer. Actual rendered frame rate depends on the device, viewport and scene. Colors passed to Core use opaque 0xAARRGGBB values. SceneView.SceneBackgroundColor accepts a MAUI Color and must be opaque. Angles are radians. Shape transforms return copies; adding a changed shape requires Scene.Replace or Scene.Add. Scene.Changed and Camera.Changed trigger a redraw automatically. Keep scene and camera mutations on the UI thread. Run the demo app or explore the examples. On Mac Catalyst, use the .NET installation with MAUI workloads and a compatible Xcode. Select the renderer SceneView.RenderingMode defaults to Auto. Select Software for the existing CPU path or Hardware to require the native GPU. Observe ActiveRenderingBackend and RenderingDiagnostic; GPU availability is established after the native surface initializes. Hardware rendering explains fallback, capture, picking and compatibility.

hardware-rendering.html.title: Software and hardware rendering | Simple3D
hardware-rendering.html.summary: Software and hardware rendering SceneView supports native Metal on iOS and Mac Catalyst and OpenGL ES 3 on Android. The hardware path uploads immutable geometry and textures once, updates transforms and lighting per draw, depth-tests triangles, and composites a selection mask only while a selected shape is visible. Other frames render in a single pass straight into the drawable or window surface. It presents native textures directly; it does not render a CPU bitmap and merely upload that bitmap to a GPU. Choose a mode The existing .UseSkiaSharp() registration remains required for software presentation and label overlays. No additional engine, browser, JavaScript bridge or registration is needed. var view = new SceneView { Scene = scene, RenderingMode = RenderingMode.Auto }; view.RenderingBackendChanged += (_, _) => System.Diagnostics.Debug.WriteLine($"{view.ActiveRenderingBackend}: {view.RenderingDiagnostic}"); view.RenderingFailed += (_, error) => System.Diagnostics.Debug.WriteLine($"{error.Message}; fallback={error.FellBackToSoftware}"); Mode Behavior Auto (default) Attempts the native GPU. Initialization or render failure selects software and records a diagnostic. Software Uses DepthRenderer and the existing adaptive CPU render resolution. Hardware Requires native GPU rendering. Failure reports None and raises RenderingFailed; no silent software fallback. Change the property on the UI thread to switch modes without rebuilding the scene or losing the camera/selection. After a failed attempt, switch to Software and back to Auto/Hardware to retry. ActiveRenderingBackend is None while waiting for a native surface or after disconnect. Merely selecting Hardware does not establish that a GPU frame succeeded. Subscribe before attaching the view to observe initialization failures. Auto's fallback stays selected until a mode change or handler reconnection; it does not repeatedly retry a failing device every frame. Only device, driver, shader and allocation failures count: scene content that cannot be prepared (exceeding the triangle or node budget) skips GPU frames and is reported in RenderingDiagnostic, and hardware rendering resumes as soon as the scene is valid again. After a failure the native surface is disconnected and its GPU resources released. Old surfaces are likewise disconnected and released when modes change. Android surface destruction drops context-owned resources and reconstructs them on surface recreation. Metal command execution errors are reported asynchronously on the UI thread. What is shared and what differs Scenes, hierarchy, materials, textures, lighting, cameras and gesture APIs are shared. Both backends support opaque geometry, Gouraud smooth lighting, vertex colors, texture addressing/filtering and selected-part highlighting. GPU selection uses a depth-tested mask and a contour one to three render pixels wide, scaled with screen density so it stays visible on high-density displays. When MaximumRenderDimension caps the render size, the frame is upscaled with linear filtering. Native graphics edge rules and rounding can differ from the software rasterizer; bitwise image equivalence is not promised. GPU geometry is expanded at upload time to preserve flat face normals, cached by immutable geometry identity, and reused across transformed shape copies. The expanded vertex data (64 bytes per triangle corner) exists only during upload; resident meshes keep no CPU copy. Resources not used by the current scene are removed from the native cache. Resident scene vertex/texture resources are capped at 256 MiB, excluding frame attachments and driver overhead. Depth is cleared and discarded each frame without being stored (memoryless on Apple GPUs; invalidated on OpenGL ES). The offscreen color and selection attachments are created the first time a selection is shown, and recreated only on resize. Node and aggregate triangle limits still apply. The CPU raster-sample budget does not constrain the GPU path. MaximumRenderDimension limits the internal GPU render target; presentation scales to the native surface. GPU rendering does not use the CPU path's 512-pixel drag limit. IsAntialiasEnabled controls software presentation only; the initial GPU backend does not enable MSAA. Normals use the transform's cofactor matrix, so very small composed scales that become singular in floating-point arithmetic still render, lighting the surviving faces like the software renderer. A shape whose transformed bounds overflow to non-finite values is skipped as a whole on the GPU, whereas the software renderer skips only its non-finite triangles. Perspective GPU projection uses an infinite far plane. Metal uses reversed depth (near = 1) with a 32-bit float buffer for precision at distance; OpenGL ES, which lacks clip control, uses a 24-bit buffer with standard depth. Orthographic geometry uses a far plane computed from scene bounds; overlay labels retain near-plane-only visibility. Animate at the display's rate SceneView draws on demand, so frame rate follows how often your app changes the scene. Drive animation with FrameClock, which ticks once per display refresh at the screen's real rate (60, 120 Hz or more; CADisplayLink on iOS and Mac Catalyst, Choreographer on Android, a timer capped at 240 Hz elsewhere): var clock = new FrameClock(); clock.Tick += (elapsed, delta) => Animate((float)elapsed.TotalSeconds); clock.Start(); // Stop() while nothing moves, so the display can slow down iPhones run apps at 60 Hz unless the app's Info.plist sets CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone to true. Android may pick a 60 Hz mode for a window on a faster screen; the gallery's MainActivity asks for the fastest mode at the current resolution. Picking, labels and snapshots Hardware picking performs an on-demand nearest-triangle ray query with near clipping and material backface culling. It does not read an ID buffer back every frame or run the full software rasterizer. Exact boundary pixels can differ from software pixel picking. Equal-depth hits prefer the earlier scene item. Large meshes can make a tap more expensive even when GPU drawing is fast. Labels are projected into a transparent Skia overlay and use the existing layout/overlap handling. They remain independent of geometry depth. In hardware mode the overlay is composited and repainted only while the scene has labels, once per GPU frame: on Android from the labels of the frame just presented, on Apple platforms in the same Core Animation transaction as the Metal frame, so labels do not trail the geometry during orbit. Lifecycle Frames requested while an iOS app is in the background are skipped and redrawn on activation; a submission rejected for background execution does not disable hardware rendering. On Android, a lost or invalidated EGL context is recreated on the same surface up to three times in a short window before the failure is reported like any other device failure. Switching RenderingMode releases the native view and all its GPU resources. Labels are drawn by a Skia overlay above the native view and stay on the GPU frame they belong to. On iOS and Mac Catalyst both repaint inside the same Core Animation commit (the overlay first, then Metal, from the same scene and camera, presented with the transaction). On Android the overlay repaints from a snapshot of the labels of the last swapped GPU frame, which the TextureView shows in the same traversal. Changes made while a Metal frame is drawing, for example a FrameSubmitted handler advancing the camera, are applied on the next run-loop turn; redrawing within the same commit would never end. CaptureFrame(width, height) deliberately remains an owned software snapshot, regardless of the view's mode. Existing capture/picking ownership remains intact; capture is not proof that the GPU works and does not include the GPU selection composite. Normal GPU painting has no pixel readback. Native validation probes explicitly wait and read pixels for comparison. Compatibility SceneView now derives from ContentView and contains its rendering surfaces. Normal Scene/Camera/selection APIs remain available, as does InvalidateSurface(). Code that cast the control to SKCanvasView or used inherited Skia paint events must be updated. There are no Windows GPU targets in this change. Validate and measure See Development and native validation. The gallery includes an Auto/Software/Hardware selector, displays the active backend or failure reason, and shows a frame-statistics HUD (FPS, frame CPU time, render size, backend, triangle count) in the scene's top-right corner. FrameSubmitted is raised on the UI thread after every frame either backend submits for display (Metal: after command-buffer commit, before the GPU finishes); counting the events gives the submission rate, which matches displayed FPS unless the platform later drops or rejects a submitted frame. Frames are drawn on demand, so a still scene raises none. LastFrameMilliseconds, LastFrameWidth and LastFrameHeight describe the last presented frame: software rasterization time, or for hardware the same value as LastHardwareSubmissionMilliseconds. LastHardwareSubmissionMilliseconds measures CPU elapsed time preparing and submitting a native frame, including any driver blocking. It is not GPU execution time or displayed FPS. For comparisons, use Release builds, the same scene/resolution and actual target devices. Headless Mesa and emulators can execute graphics APIs through software drivers; their performance numbers must not be presented as physical GPU speedups. Why GLES3 on Android initially? Vulkan is Android's primary low-level graphics API; OpenGL ES remains supported but is no longer under active feature development. This initial backend chooses GLES3 to keep native integration and maintenance small for the library's compact scenes. Vulkan offers more explicit control and lower driver overhead for demanding draw-call workloads, at the cost of explicit memory management, synchronization, swapchain handling and more device validation. The public rendering modes do not expose a graphics API and can accommodate another backend later. A future Vulkan backend should query driver capabilities at runtime and evaluate Android 10+/Vulkan 1.1 as its baseline. Earlier Android Vulkan implementations can have driver limitations. No Vulkan performance advantage is claimed without matching device measurements. See Google's Vulkan overview and native-engine guidance.

index.html.title: 3D scene renderer for .NET MAUI | Simple3D
index.html.summary: 3D scene renderer for .NET MAUI Simple3D draws opaque, depth-aware scenes on iOS, Android, and Mac Catalyst, natively on Metal or OpenGL ES 3 with a software fallback. Build scenes from boxes, spheres, cylinders, pyramids, lines, arrows, your own indexed mesh, or rigged glTF/VRM characters. Add textures, OBJ geometry, vertex colors and flat or smooth directional lighting; pose skeletons and drive facial expressions; animate at the display's full refresh rate. Place a SceneView in a MAUI page, then drag to orbit, pinch to zoom, and tap to pick the visible shape. The gallery's Mirror scene shows what this adds up to: the camera tracks a person's body and face on the device, and a skinned VRM character copies a talking, smiling face, arms and torso, and whole-body squats. The GIF shows real people from public-domain NASA/JSC and CDC videos, who do not endorse this project. Start with Getting started, then learn scenes and cameras, meshes and groups, materials, lighting and OBJ import, skinned characters and glTF, and interaction and picking. The five examples share their scene factories with the interactive app: orbit Equipment's textured controller and use Surface's shading and light controls to compare the rendering options. The API reference covers both library projects. Read Architecture and rendering pipeline for package boundaries, depth rendering, picking and buffer ownership. Use the library under the MIT license. Source and the gallery app are in the repository. Choose native GPU or software rendering.

interaction-and-picking.html.title: Interaction and picking | Simple3D
interaction-and-picking.html.summary: Interaction and picking SceneView is an SKCanvasView backed by the CPU DepthRenderer. Native painting and picking reuse a RenderTarget and Skia bitmap until their dimensions change. The target is rendered again when the bound scene, camera, background, or viewport changes. It contains packed opaque ARGB pixels, projected labels, and shape IDs for depth-aware picking. Explicit captures return owned RenderFrame snapshots. The control installs drag, pinch, and tap gestures. On Mac Catalyst, native UIKit pan and pinch recognizers handle mouse and trackpad updates without MAUI touch-count gating. Drag orbits, each pinch event applies its incremental zoom factor, and tap selects the visible leaf shape. Projected label text scales with display density. The selected leaf gets a mint tint and a gold contour inside its visible boundary. Hidden pixels remain hidden; scene materials and exported frames are unchanged. Tap the background to clear the highlight. Handle the event to show details: view.SelectionChanged += (_, shape) => details.Text = shape?.Name ?? "Nothing selected"; Set IsInteractive = false to disable built-in orbit, zoom and tap selection. Gestures your application adds to GestureRecognizers, such as a double tap command, remain installed when this property changes. Custom pointers can still call SelectAt and ClearSelection. Native label painting keeps glyphs inside the viewport and abbreviates text with an ellipsis when it cannot fit the available width. Overlapping labels move to a free nearby row, searching up to eight rows in either direction; labels without space are omitted. Earlier scene labels take priority. These adjustments affect the overlay only; Core projected anchors and picking remain unchanged. Labels still overlay geometry without depth testing. SelectAt(x, y, viewWidth, viewHeight) performs the same selection and feedback for a custom pointer. PickAt only queries; it does not change selection. Call ClearSelection() to clear the highlight from a reset command or other application action, including in display-only mode. It raises SelectionChanged with null only when a shape was selected. Scene.Replace transfers selection to the replacement node, so animated parts keep their highlight. For groups, corresponding child positions represent the same parts: preserve child order during animation. Missing children and removed shapes clear selection. SelectionChanged also reports the replacement instance, allowing details to follow changing names and values. Scene.Changed supplies ShapeReplacementEventArgs for replacements. Keep an interactive scene outside a parent ScrollView when drags should belong exclusively to the scene. The gallery places it in a flexible grid row, with scrolling confined to the scene catalogue and controls. While dragging or pinching, native rendering uses a preview capped at 512 pixels on its longest side, keeping the aspect ratio and depth picking. Scaled previews use linear sampling to soften magnified pixel steps. This filters the rendered bitmap; it is not multisample triangle rasterization. On release or cancellation the view restores its configured MaximumRenderDimension. Animation may independently use a lower configured limit. Native bitmap painting also softens high-contrast diagonal stair steps by blending perpendicular edge transitions. IsAntialiasEnabled defaults to true; set it to false to preserve unfiltered pixels or avoid the additional pixel scan on a constrained device. Straight edges and flat interiors are preserved. This filter does not change Core pixels, exported frames or picking, and it is not multisample antialiasing. Selection tint and contour are applied after the filter. For custom pointers, view.PickAt(x, y, viewWidth, viewHeight) maps layout coordinates to the last rendered frame. CaptureFrame(width, height) produces or retrieves an owned physical-pixel frame; frame.Pick(x, y) accepts physical pixels. CaptureFrame is useful for tests and exports. The renderer is not thread safe: use it and mutate its scene or camera on the same thread. The view subscribes to its current scene and camera and releases those subscriptions when its handler disconnects. Replacing either bindable property stops observing the old object. When a tap follows a scene change before the next paint, picking refreshes the frame first.

materials-and-import.html.title: Materials, lighting, and model import | Simple3D
materials-and-import.html.summary: Materials, lighting, and model import These APIs are available from 0.2.0-preview.1. Textures Texture2D copies opaque 0xFFRRGGBB pixels in row order, starting at the top-left. UV coordinates use the usual bottom-left origin: U increases rightward and V upward. Nearest sampling and clamped edges are the defaults. Bilinear filtering blends four texels; repeat addressing tiles on both axes, including negative coordinates. var texture = new Texture2D(2, 2, [0xFFFFC070, 0xFF749DFF, 0xFF749DFF, 0xFFFFC070], TextureFilter.Bilinear, TextureAddressMode.Repeat); var box = Shape.Box().WithMaterial(new Material(texture)); scene.Add(box); A texture material defaults to white, preserving the image colors. Its optional color multiplies the image, and lit: false displays it without lighting. Box and pyramid faces use planar UVs; spheres use longitude/latitude UVs; cylinders use wrapped side UVs and planar caps. Texture-ready primitive geometry is cached and shared. Use repeat addressing for tiled or seamless wrapped textures. Custom meshes supply one Vector2 texture coordinate per vertex. Duplicate vertices wherever a UV seam needs different coordinates. A textured material on a mesh without UVs throws immediately. Textured groups are rejected: apply materials to their leaves. MAUI applications can decode PNG/JPEG and other Skia-supported images without adding a dependency: using var stream = await FileSystem.OpenAppPackageFileAsync("panel.png"); var texture = TextureLoader.Load(stream, TextureFilter.Bilinear); var panel = Shape.Box().WithMaterial(new Material(texture, lit: false)); TextureLoader.Load is synchronous and leaves the stream open. Load assets once, outside animation/render callbacks; decode large images off the UI thread, then assign shapes on the UI thread. Only the first encoded image frame is loaded. Images must be fully opaque; transparent images are rejected. Dimensions are checked before decode and cannot exceed 4096 × 4096. Core itself has no image codec or file IO dependency. Directional and ambient light scene.Light = new DirectionalLight( new Vector3(.4f, -1, -.7f), // direction rays travel toward the scene color: 0xFFFFE9CF, intensity: .7f); scene.AmbientLight = .3f; The direction is world-space, finite, nonzero, and normalized on construction. Directional intensity and ambient brightness range from 0 to 1; final color channels saturate at 255. scene.Light = null disables directional lighting. Unlit materials ignore both settings. Changes notify SceneView automatically. There is one directional light and no shadow pass. Defaults preserve the original appearance: white light traveling along (.4, -.8, -1), intensity .62, ambient .38. Lighting is diffuse Lambert shading, with packed RGB arithmetic rather than a physically based, linear-light color pipeline. Smooth normals and vertex colors var mesh = new Mesh( vertices: [new Vector3(-1, -1, 0), new Vector3(1, -1, 0), new Vector3(0, 1, 0)], indices: [0, 1, 2], colors: [0xFFFFAA70, 0xFF70AAFF, 0xFF70DDC0]) .WithCalculatedNormals(); scene.Add(Shape.FromMesh(mesh, new Material(0xFFFFFFFF))); Optional normals, colors, and textureCoordinates are defensively copied and must each match the vertex count. Normals are normalized and must be finite and nonzero; colors must be opaque. Meshes without normals retain flat shading. Normals enable Gouraud shading: light and vertex color are combined at triangle corners, then interpolated across the surface. Smooth shading avoids increasing triangle count, but does not change silhouettes or add specular highlights. WithCalculatedNormals() returns a new mesh with area-weighted normals averaged at shared indices. Split vertices preserve sharp edges and UV seams; the method does not weld duplicate positions. Unused vertices or normals that cancel use +Z. Imported explicit normals are preferable when a seam should remain smooth. Nonuniform shape and group scales use inverse-transpose normal transforms. If a composed transform has no inverse but leaves a valid triangle, lighting uses its world-space face normal. Two-sided surfaces flip their lighting normals on backfaces. Colors multiply the material tint and texture. Use white material color to preserve vertex colors. UVs and shaded vertex colors use perspective-correct interpolation and are carried through near-plane clipping. Orthographic cameras interpolate linearly. The Surface example demonstrates a height gradient on 512 triangles. Its Shading (Smooth / Flat) control compares prepared meshes with and without normals; Light from (Left / Right) changes the world-space directional light without rebuilding geometry or resetting the orbit camera. OBJ geometry using var reader = new StreamReader(modelStream); var mesh = ObjReader.Read(reader); var model = Shape.FromMesh(mesh, new Material(0xFFD4DCEF)); scene.Add(model); ObjReader.Parse(string) is convenient for small embedded models. The reader supports positions, UVs, normals, positive/negative indices, triangles, and strictly convex planar polygons. It preserves independent position/UV/normal indices by splitting vertices only when attribute tuples differ. Every face corner in an input must use the same attribute layout. Explicit normals control smoothness; call WithCalculatedNormals() yourself when appropriate. Import returns one mesh. Object/group names, material references, and smoothing directives are ignored. MTL files, textures, and other external resources are never opened; assign a material yourself. Lines, points, freeform surfaces, concave/nonplanar polygons, and collinear polygon corners are rejected. Export triangulated geometry with normals and UVs from your modeling tool for predictable results. Malformed or unsupported input throws FormatException with a line number. Input is bounded to 16 Mi characters, 16 Ki characters per line, 256 corners per face, and the mesh's one-million-element limits. Supplied readers remain open. Import once, share the resulting immutable mesh, and keep IO out of animation callbacks.

meshes-and-groups.html.title: Meshes and groups | Simple3D
meshes-and-groups.html.summary: Meshes and groups A Mesh copies finite vertices and triangle indices and validates index ranges and nondegenerate faces. The same immutable mesh can be shared by many Shape.FromMesh instances. Material controls opaque color, texture, whether scene lighting applies, and whether back faces render. See materials and import for UVs, smooth normals, vertex colors, and OBJ assets. using System.Numerics; var mesh = new Mesh( [new Vector3(-1, 0, 0), new Vector3(1, 0, 0), new Vector3(0, 1, 0)], [0, 1, 2]); var face = Shape.FromMesh(mesh, new Material(0xFF86A9FF, lit: false)) .Named("Panel"); var scene = new Scene().Add(face).Add(face.At(0, 0, -1)); Shape.Group(children) applies its transform to every child. At, Rotated, and Scaled set absolute local values and return a new shape. The order is local scale, local rotation, local translation, then parent transforms. A leaf name survives picking through groups. Lines and arrows are triangle meshes, so they obey the same depth and picking rules. The surface factory builds a 16 × 16 grid with calculated smooth normals and height-based vertex colors. The executable examples render it without MAUI, and the demo adds orbit and selection.

rendering-limits.html.title: Rendering model and limits | Simple3D
rendering-limits.html.summary: Rendering model and limits The CPU raster budgets below describe the software backend. Native GPU rendering has separate resource limits, mode selection and picking behavior; see hardware rendering. DepthRenderer transforms opaque triangles, clips them at the camera near plane, shades them with configurable directional and ambient light, rasterizes with per-pixel depth, and stores the visible leaf shape for picking. This resolves intersecting opaque geometry that a sorted-triangle painter cannot. SceneRenderer remains for older primitive/default-camera code and throws a diagnostic for newer features it cannot represent. Limit Value Why Width or height 2,048 physical pixels Bounds frame storage Scene node visits 100,000 Bounds grouping traversal Aggregate triangles 1,000,000 Bounds and render traversal Raster bounding-box samples 16,000,000 per frame Bounds overlapping screen-filling work Group hierarchy 64 levels Bounds nesting The sample-work budget counts clipped triangle bounding boxes, including pixels outside the triangle but inside its box. Dense overlapping scenes can reach it before the triangle limit. Direct DepthRenderer.Render calls then throw RasterBudgetExceededException; reduce scene complexity, viewport size, or visible overlap. SceneView retries the native paint at half resolution when this happens, keeping interactive zoom usable at the cost of image sharpness. Camera.FitToScene calculates bounds before mutation and leaves the camera unchanged if a budget or overflow check fails. Repeated group instances count separately toward the node budget, including groups with no geometry. The view's resolution-recovery checks enforce this same limit, so a large replacement hierarchy cannot bypass the bound before rendering begins. Excessive node visits throw an ArgumentException; lowering render resolution does not reduce hierarchy traversal. Only opaque surfaces are supported. Labels overlay the scene and are not depth tested. There is no far clipping plane, transparency, shadowing, PBR, mipmapping, or full game engine. Opaque textures support nearest/bilinear filtering and clamp/repeat addressing. Smooth normals use per-vertex Gouraud lighting. The CPU renderer is deterministic for the tested inputs and uses a bounded scratch depth buffer. Device frame rate depends on scene, viewport, and native presentation, so profile the target device for animation. DepthRenderer.Render returns an owned RenderFrame; its pixels and picks remain valid after later renders. For repeated frames when snapshots are unnecessary, create a fixed-size RenderTarget and call RenderInto. The target reuses its pixel and picking arrays, and the next render overwrites their content. Create a new target when the viewport size changes. If rendering throws, render successfully again before reading the target. var renderer = new DepthRenderer(); var target = new RenderTarget(768, 576); renderer.RenderInto(scene, camera, target); ReadOnlyMemory<uint> pixels = target.Pixels; // Changes on the next RenderInto call. Shape? visible = target.Pick(384, 288); After its tests pass, the Core runner compares owned and reusable rendering at 768×576, including managed allocations per frame. Reuse avoids allocating full-size color and ID arrays each frame. These measurements exclude native presentation and do not establish a device frame rate. SceneView.MaximumRenderDimension controls the largest physical render dimension used during native painting. Its default is 2,048. Lower it while animating or while a scene is being manipulated, then restore it for still images. The view keeps the aspect ratio and upscales the rendered image to its layout size. Because both pixel and picking buffers scale with pixel count, changing the maximum dimension from 2,048 to 768 can substantially reduce allocation and raster work. This control does not change explicit CaptureFrame(width, height) requests. A display-only SceneView can set IsInteractive = false to release its built-in gestures. Native diagnostics The Apple demo's Debug configuration compiles the rendering libraries and framework assemblies, while retaining interpreter support for the demo assembly. Changes to compiled rendering code require a rebuild. Interpreter overhead can make Debug rendering substantially slower than the same renderer running compiled; measure the configuration you intend to use. Android Debug uses JIT compilation rather than the interpreter for the demo, including its per-pixel rendering loops. This setting is specific to the demo project. Rebuild and deploy fresh assemblies when comparing runtime performance. After building the Debug iOS simulator app, run: bash scripts/ios-simulator-smoke.sh --render-probe This runs a Debug-only check inside the native app runtime. It verifies a visible, pickable box and every gallery scene, compares owned and reusable pixels, checks retained snapshots, and measures ten camera-orbit renders per scene at 512×315. It exits before opening the gallery and shuts down its test simulator. A missing completion marker fails the script even if the launcher reports success. Timings cover Core rendering, not displayed frame rate or input latency. Run the ordinary smoke check separately to verify the actual gallery UI. Clean and rebuild native outputs after changing interpreter settings or Apple workloads so cached native assemblies do not mix configurations. Use a matching SDK, workload and Xcode combination; the Xcode 27 release instructions specify .NET SDK 10.0.401 and workload set 10.0.401.1. SceneView uses a reusable RenderTarget for native painting and picking. It reuses its Skia bitmap at the same render dimensions, copies pixels only when the target changes, and allocates a new target and bitmap when dimensions change. Explicit CaptureFrame calls still return owned snapshots. On native handler disconnect, the view releases its bitmap, reusable target, cached owned frame, and depth scratch buffer; snapshots held by callers remain valid. If a zoomed scene exceeds the raster work budget at the requested paint size, the view halves its internal render size until it can draw a frame. It keeps that size during ongoing interaction, then probes full resolution when camera or scene complexity falls or painting becomes idle. A failed probe has a short cooldown so animation does not repeat the expensive attempt every frame. RenderTarget.RasterSamples reports the bounding-box work of its last successful render; it resets to zero when a render starts or fails. Textures are bounded to 4096 pixels per dimension (up to 64 MiB of pixel storage). The public constructor copies caller pixels once into that storage; TextureLoader decodes directly into it, so codec scratch memory is the only additional allocation. OBJ input is bounded independently of frame work; see materials and import. Texture filtering and interpolated colors add per-visible-pixel work. Solid flat materials keep a separate fast pixel loop. No per-triangle heap storage is allocated by attribute clipping.

scenes-and-cameras.html.title: Scenes and cameras | Simple3D
scenes-and-cameras.html.summary: Scenes and cameras A Scene owns top-level immutable shapes and world labels. Add, Remove, Replace, AddLabel, RemoveLabel, and Clear raise a synchronous change notification after a successful mutation. A SceneView bound to the scene invalidates its cached frame. A Camera has independent yaw, pitch, distance, target, field of view, near plane, projection mode, and orthographic height; its changes invalidate the same view. var scene = new Scene().Add(Shape.Box().Named("Housing")); var camera = new Camera(5, yaw: .55f, pitch: .35f); camera.Projection = CameraProjection.Orthographic; camera.FitToScene(scene, aspectRatio: 16f / 9); view.Scene = scene; view.Camera = camera; FitToScene encloses world bounds conservatively and updates the camera atomically. Empty scenes leave the camera unchanged. Scene.GetBounds excludes labels and enforces the same aggregate triangle limit as rendering. In orthographic mode, zoom changes the visible height; in perspective mode it changes distance. Camera.Target moves the orbit center. WorldLabel positions are projected to frame pixels. Labels are overlays: they are clipped by the viewport and near plane, but they do not participate in depth testing or picking. Use them for callouts, not occluded geometry annotations.

skinned-characters.html.title: Skinned characters and glTF | Simple3D
skinned-characters.html.summary: Skinned characters and glTF Load a rigged glTF or VRM character and pose it from code: from a camera, a data stream or your own animation. The Mirror example drives a character from a person's body pose. Load a model GltfLoader reads a binary glTF 2.0 file (.glb, and VRM, which is GLB with a humanoid bone map) and decodes its textures: await using var stream = await FileSystem.OpenAppPackageFileAsync("froggy.vrm"); var character = await GltfLoader.LoadAsync(stream); // parsing and texture decoding run off the UI thread scene.Add(character.Shape); var skeleton = character.Model.Skeletons[0]; Core's GltfReader.Read does the same without decoding images, for headless rendering and tests: pass a decoder to GltfModel.CreateShape, or textured materials keep only their base color. Coordinates stay as authored: right-handed, +Y up, counterclockwise front faces. VRM 0.x models face −Z and VRM 1.0 models face +Z; Simple3D's default camera looks along −Z, so turn a VRM 0.x model with Rotated(0, MathF.PI, 0) to face it. Supported Ignored or rejected Triangle meshes, indices, normals, UV0, vertex colors Points, lines, strips (skipped) Base color factor and texture; doubleSided; KHR_materials_unlit PBR maps, alpha blending (drawn opaque), texture transforms Node hierarchy (TRS or matrix), skins with inverse bind matrices Animations, cameras, lights Morph targets on skinned primitives (POSITION/NORMAL, dense or sparse, targetNames, default weights); VRM 0.x / 1.0 expressions Morph targets on unskinned primitives, TANGENT deltas, expression material binds VRM 0.x / 1.0 humanoid bone names (GltfModel.HumanoidBones) External or data URIs, sparse accessors outside morph targets, Draco/meshopt (rejected) Input is bounded (64 MiB, Mesh.MaximumElements, node count and depth); malformed files throw InvalidDataException. Degenerate triangles are dropped. Pose a skinned shape A SkinnedMesh deforms bind-pose geometry with a Skeleton of up to 128 joints, each vertex blending up to four. A SkeletonPose sets every joint's local rotation, plus an offset for the root joints: var rotations = skeleton.RestPose.Rotations.ToArray(); var elbow = model.HumanoidBones["leftLowerArm"]; rotations[elbow] = Quaternion.CreateFromAxisAngle(Vector3.UnitZ, .8f) * rotations[elbow]; var waved = character.Shape.WithPose(SkeletonPose.Create(skeleton, rotations)); scene.Replace(character.Shape, waved); Poses and shapes are immutable like the rest of the scene: WithPose returns a copy, updating every skinned descendant that uses the pose's skeleton, and Scene.Replace redraws. SkeletonPose.WorldTransforms gives joint transforms, for example to attach a prop to a hand. SkeletonPose.Blend(from, to, amount) crossfades two poses of the same skeleton, for example to ease toward a tracked pose each displayed frame. Expressions and morph targets A SkinnedMesh carries up to 64 morph targets (blend shapes), blended before skinning. Set raw weights with Shape.WithMorphWeights(mesh, weights), or drive VRM expressions by name: var face = new Dictionary<string, float> { ["joy"] = .8f, ["a"] = mouthOpen, ["blink_l"] = 1 }; scene.Replace(current, current = character.Model.ApplyExpressions(current, face)); GltfModel.Expressions is keyed by lowercase VRM 0.x preset (joy, angry, sorrow, fun, a…o, blink, blink_l, blink_r, lookup…) or the custom name; VRM 1.0 presets keep their names and also answer to the VRM 0.x one (happy→joy, aa→a, blinkLeft→blink_l…). ApplyExpressions sums intensity × bind weight per target, clamps to [0,1], keeps pose and transforms, ignores unknown names, and shows exactly the expressions you pass: any you leave out return to neutral. Which presets exist depends on the model. Rendering cost Renderer What a new pose costs Metal / OpenGL ES 3 The bind-pose mesh uploads once and is shared by every pose and instance. Each frame uploads one joint palette (64 bytes per joint) per skinned instance; vertex shaders blend the joints. Metal / OpenGL ES 3, morphs Deltas (32 bytes per target per source vertex) upload once per mesh: a Metal buffer, or an RGBA32F texture on OpenGL ES. A weight change uploads 80 bytes of per-item constants; the vertex shader adds the 8 largest nonzero weights (more are dropped on the GPU; the software renderer blends all). Software The posed mesh is morphed and skinned on the CPU once per pose or weight change, then rasterized as usual. Picking and Scene.GetBounds use the posed geometry and skin on the CPU on demand. Lighting skins normals by the blended joint matrix, which is exact for rotations and uniform scale. Measured with the 3,330-triangle, 65-joint Mirror character on an Apple M-series Mac (Release, CPU time only): tracking, retargeting and posing take 0.02 ms per frame, preparing a 720×1280 GPU frame 0.07 ms, and a 360×640 software frame including CPU skinning 16 ms. Native probes check skinned GPU output against the software renderer, up to 128 joints, morphs at several weights on a bent pose, and that a pose or weight change uploads no vertex or delta data.
